Serock Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Serock, Poland

Demolished. Jewish settlement in Serock began at the end of the 18th century; by 1921, 2,295 Jews made up nearly half the town's population. In December 1939, Germans expelled all of Serock's Jewish residents, who were scattered to Biała Podlaska, Międzyrzec Podlaski, Łomazy, and Łuków, where most were eventually murdered. The cemetery was established around 1821-1822 and enlarged several times, reaching 1.2 hectares by 1916; early structures likely included ohels for prominent rabbis. During the war, Germans repurposed tombstones for construction, including stairs on nearby Barbarka Hill. In the 1970s, the site became part of a state-run 'Narew' Holiday Centre, complete with swings, barbecues, and gazebos - likely removing remaining tombstone traces in the process. In 1992, local activists relocated matzevot from Barbarka Hill back to the grounds, and in 2014 the site was formally fenced with a lapidarium built from preserved fragments, funded by the US Commission for the Preservation of America's Heritage Abroad and the Foundation for the Preservation of Jewish Heritage.
